content.text:
Operator
Good morning, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for standing by. Welcome, and thank you for joining the Equinor Analyst Q3 call. Throughout today's recorded presentation, all participants will be in listen-only mode. The presentation will be followed by a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, you may press star followed by one on your telephone. Please press the star key followed by zero for operator assistance. It's my pleasure, and I would now like to turn the conference over to Mr. Mads Holm, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, sir.
Mads Holm
Head of Investor Relations, Equinor
Thank you, operator. Ladies and gentlemen, I'm very pleased to welcome you to the presentation of Equinor's Q3 results call. I'm Mads Holm, Head of Investor Relations. It's my great pleasure to introduce Torgrim Reitan, who, as you know, started as CFO just a few weeks ago. For those of you unfamiliar with Torgrim, he has been with the company for 27 years and held several management positions in Norway, the United States, and the United Kingdom. His most recent position was Senior Vice President for Finance and Control in Renewables. Torgrim was a member of the Corporate Executive Committee for 10 years. First as CFO, then as Executive Vice President for Development and Production USA, and later the combined international business.
With strong experience from upstream, trading, and operations of natural gas and renewables, we are delighted to welcome Torgrim back as CFO to present Equinor's results and outlook, and to engage in the important dialogue with analysts and the investor community. Torgrim will take us through the results, and then we will open up for questions as usual. We aim to complete the call within the hour. With that, let me pass straight over to Torgrim for the presentation. Thank you very much.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Thank you, Mads, for that kind introduction, and good morning, everyone. Very good to be with you. I do look forward to meet you face-to-face, you know, at a later point in time. It's a privilege to step into this role in a company so financially solid with such a rich and attractive investment portfolio and with a clear plan for transition. Coming into this role, I have two main priorities. The first is to ensure that Equinor steers safely through these uncertain times. We see high geopolitical uncertainty, weaker prospects for global economic growth, and high volatility in the markets we operate. I want Equinor to come out of this as a stronger company. My second priority, but equally important, is to support the transition for Equinor to be a leading company as the energy transition develops.
My role will be to ensure that we continue to invest and optimize the portfolio in oil and gas, as well as grow and develop within renewable and low carbon solutions, ensuring that we focus on quality and value creation. I see our strategy as even more relevant now than before, and you should not expect any changes to the strategy as I am coming into this role. We will continue to drive value creation, which is always more important than volume targets. The numbers this quarter and for the coming quarters will be impacted by all the changes around us. One factor we will monitor closely is the inflation and cost increases. This is a growing concern. We see bottlenecks and delays, lower efficiency and risk of a drop in quality in the global supply chains.
Our sanctioned project portfolio is mostly protected from this by contract already entered into. However, our unsanctioned portfolio is exposed to changes in the supply market and in the frame conditions. For instance, the proposed change in the temporary tax regime on the Norwegian Continental Shelf will increase break-even prices for the relevant projects with $2 to 5 per barrel. Second, the outlook for commodity markets carries significant uncertainties, and we expect high volatility. Our balance sheet is robust with a net debt ratio of -19%. I ask you to note and remember that, you know, this is impacted by delayed tax payments on the NCS, the Norwegian Continental Shelf. As an example, if we paid all the taxes we owe as of today, net debt would move from -19% to within the guided range, which is +15% to 30%.
The point here is if we see a drop in commodity prices, that can quickly increase the net debt ratio. This is why capital discipline is so important. That we will prioritize in our investment portfolio, so we can execute projects with quality on time and on cost. Furthermore, maintaining a competitive capital distribution through the cycles will be very important to me. Looking at the capital distribution framework presented last year in 2021, we have used the flexibility with both significant step-ups in the share buybacks and an extraordinary dividend. We will continue to use the framework and the flexibility within it. Okay, let's turn to today's topic. We present strong results, still against a dark backdrop. Norway and Equinor's role as a supplier of energy to Europe is more important than ever.
I want to use the opportunity to thank all our employees and suppliers for all the strong efforts this quarter. We expect continued tight and volatile markets through the fall and winter. As always for European gas, temperatures and weather will have an impact. As usual for Q3, we update our commodity price assumptions. This is a slight increase in our expectations for Brent from $70 to 75 in 2025 due to limited expected supply. For European gas, we expect the TTF, you know, at $20 per MMBtu in the same year, as we expect Russian volumes to be reduced for the foreseeable future. We assume these prices will spill over to the prices for CO₂ quarters and German electricity prices.
We post adjusted earnings of more than $24 billion driven by high prices, particularly for gas, where European gas prices grew by 240% from last year, but also driven by continued high production. The production performance both at Hammerfest LNG and Peregrino, which came back on stream this summer, has been good. All the 13 LNG cargoes from Hammerfest went to Europe. By the way, so did 96% of our crude from NCS in the quarter. Peregrino phase II came on stream now in October, almost two years delayed by the corona pandemic, but it is still on budget. Gudrun phase II also came on stream, and this will contribute with a higher recovery rate and extend the tail production of that field. Talking about renewables, the first solar plant in Poland is completed.
Although energy security and production are on top of the agenda, we remain firm on our strategy and transition plans. In the quarter, we've seen Northern Lights signed its first commercial contract for CO₂ transport from the Netherlands to Øygarden outside Bergen for storage under the seabed. An important step in the development of commercial and viable value chains for CO₂. We have entered several partnerships to develop projects for large-scale commercial CO₂ storage on the Norwegian continental shelves and to develop low carbon opportunities in the United States and UK. We delivered strong financial results and with updated earnings expectations for 2022, we took a commercial decision to make an additional tax payment of around $10 billion in September. The strong results allow for continuing a competitive capital distribution.
The board has decided on a cash dividend of $0.20 per share for the Q3. On the back of the continued strong financial results, the extraordinary cash dividend is further increased from $0.50 to 0.70 per share for the Q3. This is an increase in our cash payments to shareholders of around 30% from Q2. Furthermore, we continue our share buyback program now at $6 billion for 2022. The fourth and final tranche will be around $1.8 billion with a market share of around $600 million. In total, we increase the capital distribution from $13 to 13.7 billion for 2022. We view this as a balanced approach, where we invest in our competitive portfolio and in the energy transition while showing a clear commitment to offer an attractive shareholder return.
Energy production from the Norwegian continental shelves is crucial to Europe's energy security. We have increased the state of alert based on our assessment to the threat to Equinor and as a precautionary measure. We collaborate closely with the authorities on safety and security matters. Now to safety statistics. The 12-month average serious incident frequency is 0.4, a slight improvement from last quarter. The total recordable injury frequency for the past 12 months is 2.4 per million hours worked. We deliver a high production in a quarter where we also carry out a bigger scope of seasonal turnarounds. Even with a turnaround at Oseberg, we deliver 11% more gas from the Norwegian continental shelves than in the same quarter last year.
Total gas set a production record, delivering 38 BCM, or billion cubic meters on a 100% basis in the gas year ending in September. Our total oil and gas production ended at 2,021,000bbl per day. Our production for the quarter ended at 491 GWh. 294 GWh of this production came from our renewable assets, slightly lower than last year due to maintenance activity and less wind. This summer, we acquired 50% of Triton Power in the UK, with the key plant being the Saltend Power station. Around one month of production is included in the Q3 numbers with nearly 200 GWh and $29 million in earnings, already paying down on the investment, which was $140 million for Equinor share. We continue to deliver very strong financial results.
The adjusted earnings totaled $24.3 billion, and $6.7 billion after tax. The reported net operating income was $26.1 billion and net income was $9.4 billion. We are not isolated from the cost increases impacting the rest of society. Higher energy costs, increased CO₂ tax, and price impact our operating costs, but you also see effects from longer lead times on equipment for maintenance. The cost increase is masked in our report due to substantial currency effect as we are reporting in dollars. We will continue our improvements as well as working strategically with long-term suppliers to mitigate rising cost pressure. We have net impairment reversals of $1.1 billion, mainly due to increased expectations for refinery margins and higher expected commodity prices.
We see value creation from portfolio optimization with a gain of $655 million from the divestment of our share in Ekofisk and a share in Martin Linge through Sval Energi. The tax rate in the quarter ended at 72.4%. Now let's move to the segments. Our Norwegian upstream business deliver its best results ever with adjusted earnings of $21.1 billion, and $4.7 billion after tax. High production, particularly of gas, combined with high prices drives this result. Our international business, excluding the US, performs very well in the quarter, with adjusted earnings of $942 million, and $641 million after tax. Our US upstream business delivers strong adjusted earnings of $889 million before tax and $868 million after tax.
The Midstream and Marketing segment contributes over $1.4 billion in adjusted earnings, and more than $500 million after tax. Gas, the gas pipeline network with access to many markets, combined with our marketing and trading capabilities has enabled us to create value from volatility and geographical spreads, delivering gas where it is needed the most. Excluding the positive impact of timing derivatives this quarter, the results from MMP is $1.2 billion, which is more than twice the high end of what we consider a normal result for MMP. This shows MMP's ability to deliver strong results in volatile markets. Our renewable business has negative adjusted earnings, as expected of $46 million, and -$32 million after tax. However, our producing facilities contribute with a positive result of $28 million.
In the quarter, we have a cash flow from operations of $24.5 billion. The cash flow so far this year is $62.6 billion. In August, we started tax payments based on the 2022 results. In addition to the ordinary payment of NOK 70 billion in August, we choose to make an additional payment based on commercial considerations of NOK 105 billion at the end of September. In total, we paid around $17 billion in tax in the quarter. In Q4, we will pay an additional NOK 140 billion in tax. Capital distribution in the quarter is $3.3 billion. It consists of the dividend from Q1, extraordinary dividends, and the market share of the buybacks we made in the quarter.
This also includes the state's share of share buybacks done in 2021, totaling $1.4 billion. We are doing some adjustments to our guidance. We expect a year-on-year production increase of around 1% down from the previous guidance of 2%. This is mainly explained by Johan Sverdrup phase II starting up later in Q4 than we expected. Due to its high production impact, it affects our estimates on a corporate level. We see very high volatility in the natural gas markets in Europe. For days with low prices, we will defer some production to periods where the gas is more needed and the prices are higher. As you know, we did some of this in Q2, and we will continue to use our flexibility in Q4 when appropriate.
In Q3, we have organic investments of $5.8 billion. This is somewhat lower than previously expected and impacted by removal of investments to Russia. For the year as a whole, we expect to invest around $8.5 billion. We still expect an average of about $10 billion for 2022 and 2023, and an increase to around $12 billion on average for 2024 and 2025. We will revert on this at our capital markets update in February. Thank you very much. And with that, I leave the microphone back to you, Mads, and I do look forward to your questions.
Mads Holm
Head of Investor Relations, Equinor
Thank you very much, Torgrim. Let us pass back to the operator to open up for question. Please keep in mind that no more than two questions should be asked by any participants. Thank you very much. Back to you, operator.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time, we will begin the question-and-answer session. Anyone who wishes to ask a question may press star followed by one. If you wish to remove yourself from the question queue, you may press star followed by two. Anyone who has a question may press star followed by one at this time. One moment for the first question, please. The first question is from Biraj Borkhataria from RBC. Please go ahead.
Biraj Borkhataria
Global Head of Engery Transition Research, RBC Capital Markets
Welcome back, Torgrim. I wanted to ask about the base dividend. Previously your guidance is, or the way you've talked about it is how it, you know, it grows with underlying earnings. Looking at your updated gas stat today, which is, you know, materially higher, I would have thought the underlying earnings power should also be much higher than what you would have expected previously. Could you talk about how you're thinking about the base dividend in that context? The second question is on your gas business on the NCS. In early September, there was a lot of chatter around Norway potentially agreeing a long-term fixed gas deal with Europe.
I don't expect you to talk about negotiations ongoing, but, you know, can you talk about whether Equinor would be open to this type of agreement hypothetically, and what kind of things you would need to see? Because obviously, it would give you greater clarity on your investments on the NCS as well over the long-term. Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Yeah. Thank you very much, Biraj, and good to hear from you. On your first question on the dividend, I mean, I'm very glad to see that we have been able to use the flexibility that sits within sort of the dividend policy we have, and also, I'm happy to talk about the increased extraordinary dividend, you know, for the coming quarter. You point to that, the dividend policy says that, you know, the ordinary dividend should grow in line with long-term earnings. That policy remains firm.
This is not the time to sort of, you know, make big reviews in that, but this is something that we typically do in Q4 to consider sort of the composition of the total capital distribution. If there will be changes, then natural point in time will be the Capital Markets Day in February. On sort of the question on natural gas to Europe, clearly we see that we have a very important role for the time being in providing energy to Europe in the current situation, and also providing energy to where it is needed the most.
Clearly we have optimized our production on the Norwegian continental shelf. Production permits have been increased by the government, and we have actually decided to sell natural gas instead of injecting gas as a sort of pressure support in some of the fields. Very high gas production. Of course, there are dialogues, you know, constantly with customers in many countries and different type of contract structures. I mean, we have recently signed a contract, long-term contract to Poland, and other, you know, smaller contracts as well. Many of these bilateral agreements have different type of pricing structures.
When sort of we consider those, we'll take up, you know, through commercial considerations related to that. I'm not prepared to go into any specific discussions in any specific contracts, but there's a broad range of discussions around bilateral contracts. That's right.
Biraj Borkhataria
Global Head of Engery Transition Research, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Understood. Thank you.
Operator
The next question is from Oswald Clint from Bernstein. Please go ahead.
Oswald Clint
Senior Research Analyst, Bernstein
Morning. Torgrim, hi, very good to have you back. Thank you very much. First question, just on the inflationary pressures that you were speaking about there, and I wonder if you could talk around how you're thinking about locking in rigs for perhaps the NCS, the North Sea, and I think Ulrica earlier this year was speaking about deeper supplier relationships in order to get through any inflationary pressures looking forward. Excuse me. Perhaps you could speak about what exactly you're actually doing there to perhaps mitigate some of the concerns that you were raising in your prepared remarks. And then secondly, I just wanna explore more.
I mean, Q4, Q1, normally we get a big seasonal uptick in your gas volumes, but you have been producing a lot of gas this year, sustainably through the year. The guidance still seems to suggest a decent uptick here in the fourth quarter. Are we gonna see, you know, that normal seasonal uplift with natural gas volumes through Q4, Q1? Is that still on the cards? Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Yeah. Thanks, Oswald. Yeah, good to hear from you. On the inflationary pressure, I think, you know, there are several elements to it. I mean, we see it in sort of many parts of the value chain, I mean, clearly within rigs, and I'll come back to that, but we also see it within engineering and construction, and particularly sort of in yards in Asia. We see subsea and marine activities where, you know, activity going forward will be impacted by sort of the NCS tax package. And of course, within offshore wind we see, you know, a tightness across the board.
On rigs in particular, I would say that, you know, within harsh environment, and semi-submersibles is sort of where we see probably the tightest. We work, you know, as Ulrika said, closely with those suppliers and have long-term relationships with key players. We will clearly be able to maneuver within. Maybe a little bit back to what I said in my speech, we will have to prioritize in a portfolio. So we see that we can execute, you know, our investment program with quality on time and on cost. Sort of the overall capacity in the supply chain will be a key element in that discussion.
On your second question on Q3 or Q4 and Q1 gas volumes. I think first of all, the situation in Europe is very special. You know, how demand and supply develops, you know, month-by-month is actually quite uncertain. Clearly we do see a tight market going forward, you know. In maybe some of the specifics. In Q3, we had a turnaround on Oseberg, which is a large gas producer. So that has come out of turnaround, so that will produce and have capacity available in Q4. In general, we have received increased production permits for the big gas producers from the state, also giving us the ability to continue to produce gas at a very, very high level.
I think there is something that I need to say, and that is that the gas prices fluctuate very much on a daily basis and weekly basis. We will have days and we will have weeks with very low prices, you know, in some of the locations. At those points in time, we will probably use the opportunity and the flexibility in our machine to defer gas to periods where prices are higher and the gas is needed more.
I just want to make that clear for you that, you know, we will prioritize the value over volume, in sort of, you know, optimizing our gas productions, both related to price, but also to where the gas is needed. I'm not sure if that gives a, you know, very clear answer to you as well, but the key point, it is uncertain. We have capacity available to produce very high, and we will optimize for value instead of volume.
Oswald Clint
Senior Research Analyst, Bernstein
Understood, Torgrim. Thank you very much.
Operator
The next question comes from Lydia Rainforth from Barclays. Please go ahead.
Lydia Rainforth
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Thank you very much. Torgrim, it is lovely to hear your voice again. Two questions if I could. The first one, just going back to the dividend and the extraordinary dividend. The fall off in gas prices that we've seen just sort of relatively short-term does create a potential for a fall in free cash flow for the group in Q4. How do you think about how you set that sort of extraordinary dividend? Is it done on a, this is what the results were for the quarter? Are we looking at it being slightly more stable in that sense? The second one, if I could come to the move in the accounting assumptions around the long run and the European gas price in particular.
Does that have any implications for how you think about the business, and how you think about investments going forward? Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Thank you very much, Lydia. You know, you were clicking a little bit, so maybe you can repeat the, you know, the first part on dividend for me, so I know I get the question right.
Lydia Rainforth
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Yep. Sorry about that. Yeah, I was just wondering in terms of the how you think about setting the extraordinary dividend, given how volatile the natural gas prices actually are at the moment. We obviously had it fall off from where we were at the Q3. Would that automatically translate through to a lower extraordinary dividend in the Q4? Or do you think about it being a little bit more stable? Thanks.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay, perfect. It is a very, very important question. The way we think about this is that we have, you know, we have in the policy that clearly we will have an ordinary dividend, and then we will use share buybacks to you know, in times with high prices and when we are outside sort of the guided net debt. And then we have used extraordinary dividends because we are in a situation with a very, very strong balance sheet. What you should expect is that we will do a review of the totality in relation to the Q4 and Capital Markets Update.
Clearly, there will be a clear direction that over time we will get back to the guided range on net debt. On sort of specifics on a quarter-by-quarter, we will take the approach that we will pay out dividend based on money already made, not based on expected cash flow for the future. If that gives you a little bit more steer, Lydia.
Lydia Rainforth
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Yes, that's it. Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
I hope so, yeah. The second one was related to accounting assumptions and you were clicking a little bit there as well. Maybe you can just, you know, repeat that briefly for me.
Lydia Rainforth
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Sure. I was like, we've moved into a new office and I'm not sure I know how to use the phone properly yet. It was more about, does the change in the gas prices that you've made, does it start to change how you think about the investment program and sort of how you kind of allocate capital?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay, perfect. Yeah. I mean, yeah, we have updated our assumptions related to prices, both for oil and gas, and those are assumptions that we clearly use in our processes when it comes to planning and prioritization going forward. Then as you see, it is particularly an increase in sort of the gas price for the more sort of closer years up to 2025. If anything, it sort of points investments in direction to investments that can give gas production in the short-term.
Lydia Rainforth
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barclays
Great. Thank you very much.
Operator
The next question comes from Teodor Sveen-Nilsen from SB1 Markets. Please go ahead.
Teodor Sveen-Nilsen
Equity Research Analyst, SB1 Markets
Good afternoon, Torgrim, and welcome back. Thanks for taking my questions. Two questions. First on your updated CapEx guidance. The implied CapEx guidance for 2023 is up from $10 to 11.5 billion. I just wonder how is it split between Russia, more in the portfolio and phasing, and thirdly, inflation. Second question is on Sverdrup. When specifically in Q4 do you expect Sverdrup phase II to commence production, and how should we think around the production ramp up through 2023 from Sverdrup? Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay. Thanks, Teodor. First on CapEx guidance. You're right. We have reduced CapEx guidance for the year to $8.5 billion. To give maybe a little bit more granularity into the reduction, it is not driven by sort of changes in sort of inflation because we don't see it really in sort of the reported numbers. It's driven by some delays in CapEx and that Russia is not sort of part of the guidance anymore. Russia is out and sort of we see some slight changes to Vito in the Gulf of Mexico operated by Shell and a little bit in sort of the Brazilian assets.
On top of that, we have sold a share in North Platte in Gulf of Mexico to Shell. I think those gives a more of a complete picture. Some of this is moved on to next year. We have said that the average for 2022 and 2023 will be $10 billion. Clearly we will come back to maybe more details on that in the capital market space. On Johan Sverdrup phase II. Yeah, thank you very much. Coming back as a CFO, I really appreciate Johan Sverdrup. I must allow myself to say so. Johan Sverdrup phase II, you know, have a production capacity of more than 200,000bbl per day.
It will start sort of towards the end of the quarter. Don't have a specific date for you. We do believe that it will come at full capacity during 2023. When you add together Johan Sverdrup, phase I, and phase II, you get to around 750,000 barrels per day in production, which is of course a very big contribution to earnings in 2023 and going forward. Thanks, Teodor.
Operator
The next question comes from Yoann Charenton from Société Générale. Please go ahead.
Yoann Charenton
Equity Research Analyst, Societe Generale
Hello, Torgrim. I have two questions, if you don't mind. First, one of your remarks suggested that one should account for tax payables when assessing whether the net debt ratio is actually within the targeted 15% to 30% gearing range. Just to avoid any misunderstanding, are you saying that the net debt ratio is already back within that range from your viewpoint? If so, does it mean that there is currently limited room for maintaining capital distribution above CapEx guidance next year based on the current energy price environment? Second question, if you don't mind. At the start of the year, when your predecessor presented your multi-year organic CapEx guidance, the company's project portfolio contained a few Russian projects.
You have now exited the currency, and the CapEx guidance beyond this year is maintained based on an unchanged USD, NOK exchange rate. As such, does this maintained unchanged guidance for CapEx from next year onwards capture the range of factors you touch upon in your remarks, which are basically inflation, supply chain bottlenecks, and possible changes to Norwegian development plans in response to lower tax deductions?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay. Thank you very much, Yoann. On your first question on tax payable. Let me be very clear. We currently have a net debt of -19%. The point I would like to make is that, you know, when prices are very high and earnings are very high from Norway, we will build up a tax credit position that we have to pay back over the years. Sort of as prices come down, the tax credit will be reduced. Clearly we have, I mean, we will not pay all our outstanding taxes in one go. It's just to illustrate the point. This will be a slow moving thing, and we will always have, you know, tax credits, but it will be dependent on the price level.
When we see a drop in gas and oil prices, the tax credit will go down and the net debt ratio will be higher. Then, on your question on Russia and exiting of Russia, clearly that will have an impact on sort of future outlook for the company, both when it comes to CapEx, but also production as such. We are not ready to give an update on how this will look beyond this year. All of this will come together in the Capital Markets Day that we will host in early February. I'm looking forward to see you there, Yoann.
Yoann Charenton
Equity Research Analyst, Societe Generale
Thank you, Torgrim. See you there then.
Operator
The next question comes from John Olaisen from ABG. Please go ahead.
John Olaisen
Head of Research, ABG Sundal Collier
Yes, welcome back, Torgrim. I got a question on the, let's see here what my question was actually. Related to the profitability in renewables versus oil and gas. The last couple of years, Torgrim, you've been busy with the renewable business, and probably a few people in the world knows more about profitability for projects in the renewable industry than you right now. I just wonder if you can look at right now, of course, the profitability for oil and gas are very high and for renewables is very low. I wonder if you could elaborate a little bit on where you see profitability in renewable projects right now and going forward.
Because I think that's important to bear in mind, since you have Equinor has a strong strategy of expanding in renewables. I think your view on the profitability for renewable projects would be extremely interesting to hear, please.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Thank you very much, John. Good to hear from you. It's a very important question and something clearly we discussed extensively, you know, internally as well. Maybe first, so far, you know, up to now, the renewable business have delivered actually I must allow myself to say significant value creation, you know, clearly driven by that we have accessed, you know, opportunities early. We have de-risked them, and then we have divested part of them. Actually, I think there's more than $2 billion in gains within that business. So far we have net invested $2.5 billion into that industry. I mean, it's so far actually gained quite a bit of money.
Ongoing forward and the underlying profitability in the project, yes, it is clearly lower than within the oil and gas activities, but also with a very different risk associated to it. What we see is actually that there is a lot of competition for new opportunities and seabed leases in particular. We continue to see that area and it has been so competitive that we actually have not won, you know, leases over the last year. I think we actually didn't win in four of the last leases. To be frank, I'm actually happy or not happy, I'm okay with that, because I mean the prices were too stiff, as we saw it.
We'll continue to participate, we'll continue to monitor it, and I do believe that with increasing interest rates and sort of tighter capital available, that it will sort of drive more normal economic behavior in many of these lease rounds. We take a long-term perspective on that. We have, you know, started to build more of an onshore portfolio, particularly in Europe, but also in Brazil, where we actually see that there's possible to capitalize on taking a market perspective, making money through Danske Commodities and seeing the whole power market, you know, all together. Actually promising results for many of those investments. Those are sort of you know, more short cycled investments and quicker to returns and lower capital intensity.
This is a long reply, John, but I think it will give color to what I've been doing over the last few years. What I would like to highlight as well, I mean, we see that for renewable to become a competitive business, you know, within an industry, we need to allow that business to be run differently than the oil and gas activities. We will be making changes to how we run our renewable business, still safeguarding all the big synergies that we have as being part of Equinor. Clearly we aim to capitalize on the best of both worlds. You know, giving sufficient freedom for that business to develop as needed, but really capitalizing on being part of a big and strong company like Equinor. You'll probably hear more of that, as sort of that matures.
Okay. Thank you.
John Olaisen
Head of Research, ABG Sundal Collier
Yeah. Thank you for that. Maybe I have a follow-up on that. Those two particular projects, the solar in Poland and your Brazilian projects, which also are solar. Is it possible to give us some kind of indication if those projects, the equity IRR on those projects are above the equity or the cost of equity for those projects? Is it possible to give, like, kind of a factor? Is it 20% above required equity return of those projects? Or is it below equity return, the cost of equity?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay, thanks. You know, we just installed or started our first solar asset in Poland, you know. That we are doing through sort of the Wento acquisition we did earlier on. The Brazilian assets we are developing together with Scatec. I won't go into specific returns in those, but they are within sort of the guided range that we have set related to the renewable business. On your point on equity return, you're right. These projects, particularly the one in Brazil, are project financed and then sort of equity return is driven by the leverage-
John Olaisen
Head of Research, ABG Sundal Collier
Sorry.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
That we put into these projects. Yep.
John Olaisen
Head of Research, ABG Sundal Collier
Right. That was two questions from me. The final question is regarding the CapEx. You don't make any change in your CapEx guidance. But you, as you mentioned, talk about inflation and bottlenecks. I just wonder how should we interpret that? Should we then interpret it so that it could be upside in the CapEx guidance between now and 25 if inflation comes in? Or is that already taken into account in your CapEx guidance, which you launched, if I remember correctly, a year ago or in January this year?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Yeah. Yeah. Thanks, John. I mean, what we have updated today is more on the short-term.
We will revert on an update, both in the shorter term and longer term on the Capital Markets Day. I just want to leave with you that what we see is an increased pressure in the supply value chain, both when it comes to costs and also when it comes to ability to execute, with you know, and capacity constraints. Probably nothing new compared to what you have heard from other companies.
John Olaisen
Head of Research, ABG Sundal Collier
Yeah. Okay. Thank you.
Operator
The next question comes from Martijn Rats from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.
Martijn Rats
Managing Director and Head of European Oil & Gas Equity Research, Morgan Stanley
Hi. Hello. I've got two questions so far, as well, if I may. On the issue of gas production, what you're sort of basically telling us is that sort of Equinor from now on will start to act more as a sort of a swing supplier in this market, cutting production when prices are low. But these days it's very hard to know what low really actually is, because we've seen such a wide range already. Could you speak a little bit about what you would consider to be a low price that might trigger you to actually do this? What price you would mostly then be looking at? Is it day ahead, month ahead?
I think for sort of market liquidity and those participating in gas markets, would be useful to know if there, you know, what the sort of the framework around these decisions would be also simply to help the sort of orderly working of the market. Then secondly, also related to the gas market, I wanted to ask you what you would currently consider to be the main bottleneck in supplying more gas to Europe. Is that mostly the ability to produce natural gas from the fields that you have, or is it mostly related to infrastructure bottlenecks?
Given the situation that we have and inconsistent with the revisions that you made to long-term TTF price assumptions, how you would consider about the CapEx budget specifically for gas production and infrastructure related assets? Should we expect at the capital markets day in February an increase in gas-related CapEx? Would that make sense?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay. No, very good, Martijn. Thank you very much. First of all, you know, the flexibility that we have in sort of our gas machine, as we call it, or the gas production system, is something that we have had for many, many years, and it's sort of built up deliberately for us to be able to reach various markets, and to optimize or provide gas where it's most needed, and also to give us flexibility to time the deliveries to when gas is needed and the prices are the highest. The results in the Q3 that you have seen from MMP is very much driven by. I think it's a proof point that sort of what we have built up over many, many years is really working.
It's working for Europe, and it's working for the bottom line for Equinor. On your key question, you know, being a swing supplier. Well, we will not be a swing supplier. I mean, we will produce, you know, natural gas, you know, as a base provider of energy to Europe. But on, you know, within that machine, we have flexibility, and I can give a couple of examples. We have Oseberg where you sort of have a production permit that we can produce during 80 days of a year. So we can pick the best days to produce Oseberg. So that's sort of the production permit. So that is, you know, in sort of a gas storage term, I would probably call it Europe's largest short cycle gas storage.
We have Troll, which is a very large producer. That is typically production profile from Troll is it's produced at full capacity during winter and lower during the summer. It has flexibility to move gas between summers, so it's more of a seasonal storage, if you want to compare it to sort of the storage methodology. There are a lot of other, you know, smaller flexibilities around and production permits that we can optimize and all of that. We will adjust, you know, on top of sort of the base production. We will adjust the gas production depending on when the gas is most needed in Europe and to the markets where it is most needed. Price signals is what actually dictates where the gas is needed at any point in time.
You know, NBP prices currently are significantly lower compared to what we have seen lately. Yesterday it was $6 per MMBtu and then $4, you know, the day before. Clearly that gives opportunities to defer gas. Also we are in a period where there's not a big need for additional gas to the UK. You had a question about infrastructure bottlenecks. Clearly, there are bottlenecks. I mean, infrastructure, there's a maximum capacity in all infrastructure. In total, there is flexibility to route and re-route and swap the volumes compared to the various landing points at any point in time.
Martijn Rats
Managing Director and Head of European Oil & Gas Equity Research, Morgan Stanley
Okay, thank you.
Operator
Next question is from Kim Fustier from HSBC. Please go ahead.
Kim Fustier
Senior Global Oil & Gas Analyst, HSBC
Oh, hi, Torgrim. Good to have you back. Two questions from me, please. Firstly, just going back to gas pricing mechanisms. There has been a lot of talk for many weeks now about a potential EU gas price cap. I wondered if you could share any thoughts you may have on this, particularly on the feasibility of such a cap and potential wanted or unwanted consequences. My second question is on LNG. Some of your peers are making a lot of money these days off taking US LNG and bringing it to Europe. I appreciate that you're a huge seller of pipeline gas to Europe, but you've dipped your toes into US LNG with that contract with Cheniere you signed over the summer. I was just wondering if you're considering further increasing your US LNG offtake. Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Okay. Thanks, Kim. Good to hear you. Yes, I mean, there are a lot of, you know, discussions related to efforts from the EU and mechanisms to manage a very critical energy situation for Europe. And yes, we understand that, that is a pressing issue, and that is being discussed. I think it's fair to say that, you know, anything discussed so far has not been firmed up, and there are sort of, you know, elements are moving quickly around when it comes to the various mechanisms. On a price cap in general, you know, I would say that it is important that. Well, the problem is actually it's too little energy available to Europe.
I mean, the best we can do is actually to produce more gas to Europe. That's clearly what we want to do. What we see is that sort of pricing and market prices is the best way to manage demand and supply. If we sort of make changes to well-functioning market mechanisms, we might end up in a situation where demand probably too high and it won't be able to attract the sufficient volumes to supply Europe. I think any adjustments to a well-functioning market mechanisms needs to be thought very well through. On LNG to Europe. Yeah. As you know, we have a significant gas production in the US, but in the northwest, coming out of the Marcellus area.
That is sort of serving the northeastern US markets. I mean, we have access to some re-gas capacity. It's not a big element of our earnings, but we have some. You know, we will, of course, always consider opportunities. We know that prices are volatile both on the US side and the Europe side, and the margin in between, you know, very volatile. Clearly we will take a very cautious approach in exposing us to a volatility that we can't manage.
Operator
The next question is from Amy Wong from Credit Suisse. Please go ahead.
Amy Wong
Managing Director and Head of EMEA Energy Research, Credit Suisse
Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. I just wanna hear and, you know, hear from a practitioner in renewables. In the US, you've got the Inflation Reduction Act. There's a lot of talk of more policy moving things forward. Also in Europe as well, a lot of the politicians are, you know, very vocal in terms of saying, trying to remove a lot of the obstacles and moving faster on sanctioning projects. Love to just get your thoughts as a practitioner, whether you're seeing a lot of that rhetoric really turning into action. What are you seeing on the ground there? Thank you.
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
Thank you very much, Amy. Yeah. First of all, you know, I would, you know, clearly, you know, give credit to sort of the federal offices in the US for putting forward, you know, the Inflation Reduction Act. I think it's a very, very important one, and we already see that it is attracting capital to the US. At the outset, you know, very supportive. I mean, there are several elements to it. You know, there is a minimum tax, what's it called again? Minimum, you know, tax of 15% put on sort of upstream production. That is something clearly that, when we understand the details well, will probably have an impact on going forward.
It will be effective from 1 January 2023. We will come back on the Capital Markets Day on sort of what impact that may have. On sort of the efforts pointing towards the renewable business, investment tax credit is sort of a key. You know, what we currently have is an opportunity with 30% investment tax credit, which is clearly very important for the profitability in both the Empire projects and the Beacon projects. With the new IRA, there are opportunities to qualify for a higher ITC based on sort of local content or investments, you know, at, you know, done in the US.
That will be very important, but it will take that many of the suppliers will have to establish themselves in the US to facilitate, you know, operators like us to use them. What we typically will see is sort of an inflow of investments from suppliers, and then probably also for investors like us into projects. We welcome very much, you know, the IRA on a top level.
Amy Wong
Managing Director and Head of EMEA Energy Research, Credit Suisse
Just a quick follow-up on your comments on Empire and Beacon. Would those tax credits actually, you know, move the dial in terms of your IRRs in the projects?
Torgrim Reitan
CFO and EVP, Equinor
I mean, the use of the investment tax credits are important for the returns in those projects. The higher the ITC credits, the better returns.
Amy Wong
Managing Director and Head of EMEA Energy Research, Credit Suisse
Okay. Thank you. I'll turn it over.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, in the interest of time, we have to end the Q&A session now, and I hand back to Mr. Mads Holm for closing comments.
Mads Holm
Head of Investor Relations, Equinor
Thank you, operator. Thank you, Torgrim, and thank you all for your time this morning. As always, if there's any further questions that you have, please contact Investor Relations team on the usual numbers, and we'll get back to you as soon as we can. Also, please note that we plan to host a virtual gas market update 14 November 2022, 3:00PM CET. Once again, thank you for your time and have a great day. Thank you.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, the conference is now concluded, and you may disconnect your telephone. Thank you very much for joining, and have a pleasant day. Goodbye.

Usikkerhet for den økonomiske utviklingen. Når Kina åpner opp etter COVID, vil de også drive opp aktivitet og energietterspørsel. Det er vanskelig å spå, ikke minst om framtida, men vi vet at det er lite ekstra kapasitet på tilbudssiden. Selv om OPEC økte produksjonskvotene, har flere land meldt at de ikke har kapasitet til å oppfylle disse. Vi vet at både husholdninger og industri trenger energi fremover. Dette understreker behovet for økte investeringer i alle deler av energisektoren. Vårt viktigste bidrag akkurat nå er å sikre stabile leveranser av energi, samtidig som vi fortsetter å investere i energiomstillingen. Vi forbereder oss på fortsatt stor usikkerhet og svingninger og bygge robusthet og handlingsrom gjennom kapital og kostnadsdisiplin. Med dette krevende bakteppet så leverer vi svært sterke finansielle resultater. Kontantstrømmen etter driften etter skatt er på $10 billion.
I høst og i vinter satte vi i verk flere tiltak for å øke gassleveransene til Europa. Vi har opprettholdt den ekstraordinært høye gassproduksjonen inn i Q2. Et kvartal som vi normalt sett produserer mindre gass. Totalt produserte vi 18% mer gass på norsk sokkel enn i samme kvartal i fjor. Kun 4% ned fra Q1 i år. Høy produksjon om sommeren er et viktig bidrag til at Europa får fylt opp sine gasslagre. Etter omfattende reparasjoner, forbedringsarbeid og vedlikehold kom Hammerfest LNG trygt tilbake i drift 1 June. De første lastene gikk til Nederland, Italia, Litauen, og Frankrike. Også oljeproduksjonen vår bidrar til den europeiske energisikkerheten. Av lastene fra norsk sokkel i kvartalet gikk nærmest alle til Europa. Forrige uke da kom også Peregrino feltet tilbake i drift. Det har vært en krevende prosess fordi Brasil fortsatt er påvirket av covid og restriksjoner.
I kvartalet har vi god industriell framdrift i tråd med strategien vår. Vi gjennomførte flere verdiskapende transaksjoner både på norsk sokkel og internasjonalt. La meg få lov til å trekke fram et par av disse. På norsk sokkel fullførte vi i kvartalet kjøp av andeler i Statfjord. Vi økte vår andel i feltet med effekt fra 1 January, og med de høye prisene mottok vi faktisk betaling ved fullføringen av kjøpet. I USA tok vi over hele eierskapet i North Platte før vi solgte andeler og overførte operatørskapet til Shell. Samlet sett sitter vi igjen med økt andel i feltet og en betaling fra Shell. Vi har også trekt oss ut av alle eierandeler i Russland, slik som vi varslet. Vi har hatt god framdrift i arbeidet med nye verdikjeder for kraft.
Sammen med SSE har vi kjøpt energiselskapet Triton Power i Storbritannia. Triton sitt gasskraftanlegg i Saltend er en viktig del av dette. Her vil vi forberede anlegget til å kunne bruke hydrogen i kraftproduksjonen på sikt. I USA så har vi kjøpt East Point Energy, et selskap som utvikler og selger batteriparkprosjekter. Energilagring er en viktig og nødvendig del av overgangen til et mer fornybar energi, og andre lavkarbonkjeder. I starten av kvartalet så ble vi tildelt CO2-lagringslisens for Smeaheia. Dette prosjektet vil ha en lagringskapasitet på 20 millioner tonn årlig, og sammen med belgiske Fluxys skal vi studere muligheten for rørtransport av CO2 fra kontinentet til sikker lagring på norsk sokkel. Storskala CO2-lagring er et, og et kommersielt marked for CO2, er nødvendig om verden skal nå målet om netto nullutslipp innen 2050.
Vi leverer svært sterke resultater og bygger robusthet med en sterk balanse. Styret har besluttet et kontantutbytte på $0.20 per aksje for Q2. På bakgrunn av de sterke finansielle resultatene fra H1 økes det ekstraordinære kontantutbyttet fra $0.20 til $0.50 per aksje for Q2 og Q3. Tilbakekjøpsprogrammet vårt bygger på forutsetninger om oljeprisen, gjeldsgraden og råvareprisene. Vi øker nå tilbakekjøpsprogrammet fra $5 billion til opptil $6 billion for 2022. Tredje transje blir på $1.8 billion, der aksjer for en verdi av om lag $600 million handles i markedet. Totalt sett så øker vi kapitaldistribusjonen til våre eiere fra $10 billion til opptil $13 billion i 2022. Dette mener vi gir en god balanse der vi investerer i energiomstillingen, samtidig som vi leverer en attraktiv avkastning til våre aksjonærer.
De siste tolv månedene er frekvensen for alvorlige hendelser på 0.5. Fallende gjenstander utgjorde flesteparten av de alvorlige hendelsene i Q2. Personskadefrekvensen de siste tolv månedene er på 2.5 per million arbeidstimer. Det er en liten økning som vi tar på stort alvor. Vi jobber tett med partnere, leverandører, tillitsvalgte, verneapparat, og andre for å lære sammen og av hverandre. Forebygging av fallende gjenstander er fokuset i perioden fremover. Det skal være trygt å jobbe for Equinor. Vi leverer stabil og god drift i kvartalet for olje og gass samt for kraft. Samlet olje- og gassproduksjon var 1,984,000 fat per dag. Justert for salg av Bakken og eierandelene i Russland er produksjonen litt over 1% høyere enn Q2 i fjor. Nå i Q3 skal vi gjennomføre planlagt vedlikehold for Oseberg.
Dette vil påvirke gassvolumet, men vi fortsetter å prioritere høye gassleveranser med de tiltakene som er iverksatt. Martin Linge fortsatte opptrappingen i kvartalet, og i løpet av året vil både Johan Sverdrup fase to, Njord Future og Peregrino fase to starte produksjon. Vi har økt kraftproduksjonen fra samme kvartalet i fjor til 325 gigawattimer. Solkraftanlegget i Argentina bidrar mest til den økningen, men også havvindparkene produserer mer. Flaskehalser i globale verdikjeder påvirker hele industrien. Vi har god framdrift på havvindprosjektene, men måtte justere planen for Hywind Tampen grunnet flaskehalser knyttet til leveranser av stål. 4 turbiner er allerede installert på feltet, og totalt 7 vil komme i produksjon i år. De siste 4 turbinene rekker ikke årets værvindu og må installeres til våren. Selv med bare 7 turbiner installert vil Hywind Tampen med 60MW kapasitet være verdens største flytende havvindspark.
Vi fortsetter å levere svært sterke finansielle resultater. Justert driftsresultat er på $17.6 billion og $5 billion etter skatt. Det rapporterte driftsresultatet endte på $17.7 billion, og resultatet etter skatt ble $6.8 billion. Høyere inflasjon og økte priser verden over merkes også hos oss. Sammen med høyere priser for strøm og økte CO2 avgifter gir dette økte kostnader. Vi fortsetter forbedringsarbeidet og for å holde kostnadene under kontroll og dempe effekten av prisvekst. Skatteraten ble på 71.6% på det justerte resultatet og er påvirket av at en stor del av resultatet kommer fra norsk sokkel. Her er høy skatterate et tydelig tegn på gode resultater. Over til segmentene. Vår norske oppstrømsvirksomhet leverer de beste tallene for Q2 noen sinne. Justert resultat ble $14 billion og over $3 billion etter skatt.
Stabil og god drift samt høy gassproduksjon gjør at vi skaper store verdier på norsk sokkel. Her ser vi at både strømpris og høyere CO2 kostnader samt annen prisvekst drar kostnadene opp. Dette dempes noe av en sterkere dollar. Vår internasjonale virksomhet gjør det svært godt i dette kvartalet med god inntjening og kostnadskontroll. Samlet sett har vår internasjonale virksomhet aldri levert så sterke resultater. Vår internasjonale oppstrømsvirksomhet utenfor USA leverer et justert resultat på over $1.1 billion før skatt og $700 million etter skatt. Oppstrømsvirksomheten i USA leverer rekordresultater selv med noe lavere produksjon. Justert resultat er på nesten $900 million, mens kontantstrømmen er på $1.1 billion. Midtstrøms og markedsføringssegmentet bidrar med et sterkt resultat på om lag $1.3 billion. Gode resultater fra salg og trading av europeisk gass og elektrisk kraft bidrar sterkt.
Vi har i tidligere kvartaler snakket en del om prissikringsmekanismene som vi bruker. I dette kvartalet gir de positiv effekt for MMP resultatet. Fornybarvirksomheten vår leverer et justert resultat på -$42 million. Våre anlegg i drift bidrar med et resultat på +$32 million. Kontantstrømmen fra driften etter skatt er på $10 billion. For H1 er dette på $66 billion. Skatteinnbetalinger på norsk sokkel utgjør $73 billion i kvartalet. I H1 har vi betalt nær $110 billion i skatt basert på 2021 resultatene. Fra høsten vil skatteinnbetalingene være basert på 2022 resultatene og det nye skatteregimet som Stortinget vedtok før sommeren. I Q3 har vi en skatteinnbetaling for norsk sokkel, og den alene er på om lag NOK 70 billion. Kapitaldistribusjon i kvartalet er på $1.6 billion, og det består av utbytte fra Q4.
Ekstraordinært utbytte og markedsandelen av tilbakekjøpene vi gjennomførte i mai og juni. Tilbakekjøp av aksjer fra staten for å holde statens eierandel stabil. Den gjøres årlig. I forrige uke betalte vi for statens andel av tilbakekjøp gjort i 2021 og Q1. Totalt betalte vi over NOK 13.5 billion, og dette vil påvirke kontantstrømmen i Q3. Etter skatteinnbetalinger og kapitaldistribusjon blir netto kontantstrøm for Q2 $7 billion. Dette styrker balansen videre til en gjeldsgrad på -33.6%. Men husk at vi har utestående skatt på $22 billion, og i tillegg har vi kommende utbetalinger av utbytte. Ikke minst vi investerer for framtiden gjennom en god prosjektportefølje. Med den store usikkerheten som er i markedet, er det godt å være solide. Det er vi. Vi har stø kurs og gjør ingen endringer i guidingen vår.
Så langt i år har vi investert $3.8 billion. Vi forventer å investere om lag $10 billion i gjennomsnitt i år og neste år, men vektet mer mot neste år. Med det gir jeg ordet tilbake til deg, Sissel, og ser frem til spørsmål.
Tusen takk skal du ha! Da vil jeg minne om at de som er med på Zoom, dere må presentere dere, så kan dere stille spørsmål når jeg gir dere ordet. Dere som er her i salen, dere har fått mikrofoner, så det er fint om dere bruker de mikrofonene fordi da kan de som følger med digitalt også høre spørsmålene deres. Så er det veldig kjekt å se at flere nye fjes her i dag, og da er det fint om dere introduserer dere selv før dere stiller spørsmål, så vet vi hvor dere kommer fra. Okay, da setter vi i gang. Da ser Anders Librenne fra Førstemann ut.
Hvordan påvirkes strømprisen i Norge av aktiviteten deres? Dere skriver tre ganger i det dokumentet at høye strømpriser påvirker kostnadene. I hvilken grad gjør det det?
Det er jo fordi at vi har elektrifisert deler av sokkelen, Johan Sverdrup, Martin Linge, Troll, og vi betaler jo strømpriser også for bruken av den strømmen, og det har gjort at vi har hatt økte kostnader, for strøm. Så vet vi jo at det er viktig å elektrifisere sokkelen i forhold til å nå klimamålene våre. Så er det også begrensninger for strøm fra land i årene fremover. Derfor har vi foreslått blant annet en havvindpark utenfor Troll for å være med og bidra til å balansere strømproduksjonen i Norge.
Det er frykt for strømrasjonering nå. Er dere bekymret for at det kan gå ut over aktiviteten deres på norsk sokkel og deres evne til å levere olje og gass til Europa?
Dette er noe som vi følger veldig tett og vil jo ha en tett dialog med departementet i forhold til om det skulle komme til det, den situasjonen at det blir rasjonering. Da må jo norske myndigheter gjøre de vurderingene som skal til for å prioritere, hva som skal få strøm. Vi følger dette veldig tett, men det er for tidlig å si noe om hva konsekvensene blir.
Ja, da er det flere spørsmål i plenum. Ja, vær så god. Bak der.
Hallo. Ja. Hei, det var Marit Selgelid Larsen, NTB. Dere har veldig mye penger på bok. Hva skal dere gjøre med de fremover? Blir det noen store nye grønne investeringer, eller hva er planen?
Nå har jo vi lagt fram en energitransisjonsplan, og vi har lagt fram en strategi som viser vår satsing innenfor å være en deltager i det grønne skiftet og energiomstillingen blant annet. For et år siden la vi fram strategien der vi sa at vi ser for oss å bruke opptil $37 billion fram til 2026 på våre fornybare investeringer. Vi følger den planen, og vi leter stadig etter nye prosjekter. Når det gjelder pengene, så sa jeg som sagt at vi investerer i prosjekter. Vi investerer i prosjekter, vi skal betale en stor del av skatt og så utbytte. Vi har faktisk muligheter til å gjøre alle disse tingene, samtidig også å lete etter nye gode vekstmuligheter.
Da er neste spørsmål fra Hermann Mostu Montell.
Hei. Jeg har et spørsmål angående Europa. Tror du Europa klarer seg gjennom denne vinteren med lavere gassleveranser fra Russland?
Nå er jo på en måte den store jokeren da. Hva blir gassleveransene fra Russland gjennom vinteren? Vi har fokus på det vi kan gjøre, og det har vært også på en måte sammen med norske myndigheter, sammen med andre operatører på norsk sokkel, å produsere så mye gass som mulig. Gassco får så mye gass gjennom rørene som mulig. Det er det vi kan gjøre og være en leverandør som Europa kan stole på. Equinor har jo blitt Europas viktigste leverandør av energi, gjennom denne konflikten, og derfor så betyr kanskje det at vi har sikker og effektiv drift betyr veldig mye.
Her gjør våre ansatte en fantastisk jobb både på land og til havs for å sørge for at driften, nye brønner og nye prosjekter kommer på plass, slik at vi kan være en positiv bidragsyter i denne vanskelige situasjonen. Så gjenstår det å se. Klarer vi å få nok på lager? Hva blir gassproduksjonen, gassen som kommer fra Russland? Vi skal i hvert fall gjøre det som vi kan fra vår side, og det skal vi bidra med.
Det at EU skal kutte gassbruken med 15%, hvordan vil det påvirke, altså salg, gassalget fra Equinor? Kan det innebære reduserte gassleveranser?
Nei, altså, vi kommer nok til å produsere for fullt det vi kan fremover uansett. Vi ser jo at Europa mangler gass. Problemene startet jo i fjor sommer egentlig, for Europa har jo ikke muligheten til å levere gass fra sitt interne marked. De er helt avhengige av gass utenfra, og de har vært helt avhengig av Norge, Russland og LNG. Og med reduserte volumer fra Russland så er det Norge og LNG og noen andre land som kan øke littegrann, som en må stole på. Derfor ja, det blir veldig vanskelig å spå om denne vinteren. Men at det blir en krevende vinter for Europa, det er helt klart.
Ja. Mikael Holter fra Dagens Næringsliv.
Takk skal du ha. Et par oppfølgingsspørsmål på gass. Det første på kort sikt. Det er blitt sagt flere ganger, både fra deres side og fra norske myndigheters side, at nå produserer jo Norge og oljeselskapene på norsk sokkel mer eller mindre for fullt. Eksporten likedan. Er det sånn at dere ser på muligheter for å øke det ytterligere med nye grep som det ennå ikke har vært snakket om?
Altså, som jeg har sagt så startet disse problemene eller utfordringene i gassleveranser til Europa for et år siden, og vi har jo jobbet intenst med norske myndigheter internt i selskapet, med andre operatører og Gassco for å gjøre alle de kortsiktige løsningene som kan gjøres. Det som det handler om nå, det er at vi leter. I fjor så sa vi at vi skulle ha 50 til 30 letebrønner på norsk sokkel. Vi leter jo også etter gass. Og så handler det om å se og gjøre funn og få disse inn i systemet.
Ikke minst blir dette viktig i forhold til det langsiktige med å få et hydrogensamfunn der norsk gass nok kommer til å spille en viktig rolle for Europa, vi kommer til å ha både grønn og blå hydrogen, men det tar lang tid å få store volumer av grønn hydrogen, og der kan blå hydrogen basert på gass og CO2 lagring fra Norge være en stor bidragsyter. Derfor har vi fokus også på gass i det lange løp.
Netop på litt lengre sikt. EU kom, Europakommisjonen kom jo med en ganske kraftig uttalelse i som støtter videre leting og investeringer i på norsk sokkel. Er det sånn at disse signalene fra EU gir nye muligheter på for Equinor og andre oljeselskaper på norsk sokkel, som for eksempel muligheten til å bygge et gassrør fra Barentshavet og ned til det eksisterende systemet?
Når vi la fram strategien for et år siden, så jo vi at energiknappheten var en mulighet, og derfor la vi fram en ambisiøs plan både med prosjekter innenfor olje, gass og fornybar. Ikke minst økte vi letingen på norsk sokkel. At EU har disse behovene, kom ikke som en overraskelse for oss. Det nye er nå at det er mye mer uttalt enn det var for et år siden, der mange snakket om at ingen ny leting, nye felt var nødvendig. Det viser seg at det er det faktisk likevel. Samtidig ser vi jo at EU er veldig bevisst på at energisikkerhet ikke bare betyr å investere i mer olje og gass og lange kontrakter på gass for eksempel. Det betyr også mer investeringer på fornybar.
Det betyr at vi må balansere dette fremover, for Europa kommer til å bli et stort fornybarmarked, spesielt innenfor transport og lagring av CO2 i forhold til blå hydrogen og ikke minst offshore vind med deres nye ambisjoner. Jeg tror hvis en går litt nærmere inn på EU sine planer, så vil en også se at dette er et balansert utspill fra EU, og det driver nødvendigvis ikke veldig lange investeringshorisonter på olje og gass og for eksempel et rør til Barentshavet. Her er vi jo i tett dialog med både Brussel og Berlin, og vi blir jo lyttet til i disse dager og har god dialog med politikerne i de aktuelle landene.
Du har ikke endret ditt syn nevneverdig, det som er kommet av signaler nå i det siste?
Det har vel mer bekreftet det som vi har lagt til grunn i vår strategi at en må fortsette å investere i olje og gass også på lengre sikt, samtidig som en må øke investeringene i fornybar og lavkarbonløsninger. Det er det vi la fram for et år siden, og som ligger inne i energitransisjonsplanen.
Tillat meg et siste om gass. Vi har jo skrevet i det om Linnorm-prosjektet der det er uenighet mellom blant annet operatør Shell og Equinor. Dette handler om et gassfelt som kunne etter planen komme til produksjon i 2026 med relativt store gassvolumer til det europeiske markedet. Shell mener i alle fall at dette ville økt Norges gasseksportkapasitet. Likevel så er det sånn at dere synes å foretrekke en løsning der denne gassen kommer til markedet først på 2030-tallet. Kan du forklare dere som jo sier at dere leter aktivt etter gass nå og formodentlig har lyst til å finne gass og å få det inn i systemet i årene som kommer. Hvorfor er det ikke Linnorm-prosjektet og det konseptet som har ligget på bordet en stund, godt nok for Equinor?
Nå er det sånn at uansett hvilket marked vi har, så vil jo vi alltid sikre oss at de prosjektene vi investerer i skal være lønnsomme, og de skal være robuste i forhold til våre vurderinger. Norsk oljepolitikk er jo sånn at det er flere lisensinnehavere på hver enkelt lisens, nettopp for å skape en dynamikk og en dialog om hva som er den beste utbyggingsløsningen. Det har vi også hatt på Linnorm. Det er ikke noe dramatikk i at det er uenighet om en utbyggingsløsning, det har vi hatt mange ganger på norsk sokkel, og så har vi litt ulikt syn på kan du si utbyggingsløsning, lønnsomhet, robusthet, og så videre, og det har vi tatt inn i vår vurdering av Linnorm. Dette har ingenting med vår vurdering av gassmarkedet eller vår fokus på å levere gass til Europa.
Det har også med å gjøre en vurdering av hvert enkelt prosjekt og gi de innspillene som til operatøren.
Dere mener rett og slett at det konseptet som har ligget på bordet ikke er lønnsomt eller robust nok?
Altså, vi har bare gjort en vurdering som alle andre selskaper har gjort på Linnorm, og så har vi gitt vår vurdering til operatøren, og vi mener at kanskje et annet konsept er det som vi bør se nærmere på.
Ja, nå ser jeg ingen flere spørsmål her i salen, og det er heller ingen spørsmål på Zoom. Med det så avslutter vi denne seansen, og så tar vi noen en til en intervjuer etterpå. Tusen takk for nå.
